subject: Architecture
title: Seismic Design: Shaking Without Breaking
description: A micro-lesson that makes Seismic Design: Shaking Without Breaking usable.

hook.text: Japan builds skyscrapers that sway four feet during earthquakes — and nobody inside gets hurt.

buildup.text: Base isolation places buildings on rubber pads or rollers — letting the ground shake while the building stays still.

discovery.text: Tuned mass dampers — giant pendulums near the top — counterswing to reduce building motion during quakes.

twist.text: Chile's 2010 earthquake was 500 times stronger than Haiti's 2010 quake — but killed 99.7% fewer people. Codes matter.

climax.text: Taipei 101's 730-ton pendulum is visible to tourists — the engineering is the attraction.

punchline.text: The building doesn't fight the earthquake. It dances with it.

quiz.question: How do base isolation systems protect buildings during earthquakes?
options: They anchor the building deeper into bedrock
Rubber pads let the ground move while the building stays still
Steel braces lock the structure rigid against motion

details.summary: Seismic design engineers buildings to survive earthquakes through flexibility rather than rigidity. Base isolation, tuned mass dampers, and ductile detailing allow structures to sway and absorb energy without collapsing.
details.whyItMatters: Earthquakes don't kill people — collapsed buildings do. Seismic design is the difference between Japan's survival of magnitude 9 quakes and catastrophic death tolls in countries with inadequate building codes.
takeaways: Seismic design uses flexibility to survive earthquake forces
Base isolation and dampers let buildings sway without collapse
Each major earthquake reveals new lessons for building codes

faq.question: How does base isolation work?
faq.answer: The building sits on rubber-and-steel bearings or sliding surfaces that decouple it from ground motion. During an earthquake, the ground shakes but the building glides smoothly above it, reducing forces transmitted to the structure by 75-90%. It's like putting the building on roller skates.

faq.question: Why do modern buildings survive earthquakes that destroy older ones?
faq.answer: Modern seismic codes require ductile detailing — reinforcing steel and concrete connections that bend without breaking. Older buildings often use brittle materials and connections that snap under seismic forces.
